members.name: Environmental sensors
members.unreachableHelp: The SIEC sensor server could not be reached. If you are signed in, try again later; otherwise use Sign in for sensor data at the top of the map.
members.description:
**Full title:** SenseH2O / Forth-ERA sensors (live)

Live sensors from the SIEC Forth-ERA network (the data behind the SenseH2O app) in and around the Almond catchment, read through a small helper on this computer that signs in to SIEC. Readings from the last 7 days are averaged by hour. Pick a parameter under Display Variable to colour every site by its value, and use the time slider to step through the hours. A light grey circle means that site has no reading for that parameter in that hour. Click a site to see all of its parameters, each with a chart of the week's readings. Battery and signal readings are left out. Monthly MOT sampling results are in their own layer under River health and pressures. For interactive charts and comparisons between sites, use the [sensor explorer](sensors/).
members.attribution: Sensor data: SIEC Forth-ERA (Scotland's International Environment Centre).

catalog.name: River health and pressures
catalog.description: SEPA classification of the river's health and the pressures on it.

members.name: River health zones
members.description:
**Full title:** River health zones (live)

The river split into three stretches, Upper, Middle and Lower Almond. Each is rated Red, Amber or Green every 15 minutes from the live flow at its SEPA gauge compared with that gauge's own long-term record: Green is a normal flow, Amber is low or high, Red is very low (drought stress) or very high (flood). Click a zone for its ecological health, pressures, and what you can do.

There is no live water-quality feed for the Almond in SEPA's open services, so this rating is about flow only.

<collapsible title="Did you know?" open="true">

- This stretch drains **{{area_km2}} km²** of land, and every drain, field and road in it ends up in me.
- There are **{{barriers}} recorded obstacles to fish passage** here, such as weirs and culverts.
- SEPA has **{{permits}} water permits** in this stretch, **{{sewage_permits}}** of them for sewage discharges or overflows.
- My flow here is usually between **{{flow_q70}}** and **{{flow_q30}}** m³/s. It drops below **{{flow_q95}}** only 5% of the time and goes above **{{flow_q10}}** 10% of the time.

</collapsible>

<collapsible title="Find out more">

- [Live level and flow at {{gauge_name}} (SEPA)](https://www2.sepa.org.uk/waterlevels/default.aspx?sd=t&lc={{gauge}})
- [SEPA water classification hub](https://informatics.sepa.org.uk/WaterClassificationHub/)
- [SEPA Floodline: flood alerts and warnings](https://floodline.sepa.org.uk/)
- Turn on *Discharge and engineering permits* and *Obstacles to fish passage* to see the pressures on this stretch.

</collapsible>

<collapsible title="What you can do">

- Only rain down the drain: no oil, paint or soapy car-wash water in street drains.
- Bin wipes, cotton buds and fats instead of flushing them. They cause sewer blockages and overflows.
- Seen pollution, a dead fish or an odd colour? Report it to SEPA (0800 80 70 60, 24 hours), and use **Report what you see** on this map.
- Sign up for SEPA Floodline alerts if you live or work near me.

</collapsible>

members.description:
**Full title:** Monthly water sampling (Forth-ERA MOT)

Monthly water-quality sampling results (the MOT datastreams in the SIEC Forth-ERA SensorThings service). These are periodic samples, not live sensors. Pick a parameter under Display Variable to colour every site by its result, and use the time slider to step through the months (the last 24 months are loaded). A light grey circle means that site has no result for that parameter in that month. Read through the same local helper as the live SenseH2O sensors. Click a site to see all of its parameters, each with a chart of its results over time. For interactive charts and comparisons between sites, use the [sensor explorer](sensors/).

stories.title: Hi, I'm the River Almond
stories.text:
Hi, I'm the River Almond. I start as small burns on the moors near Harthill and Cobbinshaw and flow east past Whitburn, Livingston and Kirkliston, to meet the Firth of Forth at Cramond.

About 385 km² of land drains into me. The dark blue line is my catchment: every drop of rain that falls inside it ends up in me.

Let's follow Jenna, who lives in Livingston and loves paddleboarding and walking her dog along my banks.

stories.title: How I'm feeling today
stories.text:
These dots are my live gauges. SEPA measures my level, and the rainfall on my catchment, every 15 minutes.

Blue means I'm at a normal level. Orange and red mean I'm rising towards the kind of peak I usually reach about once a year.

The shaded areas are my three stretches, Upper, Middle and Lower. Each is coloured by how I'm flowing there right now: green is normal, amber is low or high, red is very low or very high.

Click a stretch or any gauge to see my last 7 days as a chart.

stories.title: Jenna checks on me in Livingston
stories.text:
Jenna wants to paddle near Almondell this weekend. For her, two things matter: how fast I'm flowing and how clear I am.

The Almondell gauge, just downstream of Livingston, tells her whether I'm sluggish, steady or running high. After heavy rain I can rise quickly here, so it's worth checking before she gets in.

stories.title: What's building up inside me
stories.text:
Today Jenna notices I look murky, and wants to know why.

SEPA checks the health of each stretch of river. In 2024, 18 of my 20 stretches were rated Poor; only 2 were Good. The colours on the map show each stretch and the land that drains into it.

One of the things that can hold me back is phosphorus. It comes from treated and untreated wastewater, from farmland after heavy rain, and from everyday products washed down drains. Too much of it feeds algae, which clouds my water and uses up oxygen my fish need.

The small dots are SEPA water permits. The dark red ones are public sewage treatment works and overflows.

Click a stretch to open SEPA's classification sheet for it, or a dot to see what the permit is for.

stories.title: Watch a storm hit me
stories.text:
Here's a real storm: 23 to 26 October 2026, played back an hour every second or so.

The blue circles are rain gauges; the bigger they grow, the harder it's raining. The coloured dots are my river gauges: green is normal, orange and red mean I'm close to my usual yearly peak. Whitburn, near my source, reached it.

Watch the red dots: each one is a sewer overflow spilling into me. At least 49 spilled during this storm.

stories.title: When it rains hard
stories.text:
When heavy rain falls on my catchment, I can burst my banks.

The blue areas are SEPA's flood maps: dark blue has a 1 in 10 chance of flooding each year, lighter blue a 1 in 200 chance. Here in Livingston and Mid Calder, the land closest to me is the first to flood.

Heavy rain can also overwhelm sewers, which then spill into me through overflows. That's one reason my water quality can drop after a storm.

stories.title: Barriers in my way
stories.text:
Salmon and sea trout need to swim up and down me, but weirs, culverts and bridges get in the way. SEPA records 66 obstacles to fish passage in my catchment.

The coloured lines show how much each stretch has been physically changed by people (straightened, walled in or culverted). The more modified I am, the fewer places wildlife has to live.

stories.title: How you can help me
stories.text:
Jenna goes home knowing a bit more about me, and a few things she can do:

  • Only flush the 3Ps (pee, poo and paper). Wipes and fat block sewers and cause spills.
  • Report pollution, odd colours or dead fish to SEPA on 0800 80 70 60, any time.
  • Check your home's plumbing isn't misconnected, sending washing-machine water into a surface drain that leads straight to me.
  • Join a river clean-up or citizen science group with the Forth Rivers Trust.

Thanks for spending time with me. Close this panel to explore the map yourself.
